questions.question: Bathini Deliveries' vehicles: opening cost R1 400 000 and accumulated depreciation R560 000; additions R400 000; a disposal with cost R200 000 and accumulated depreciation R140 000, sold for R48 000; depreciation for the year R230 000. Complete the fixed asset note and state what appears in the income statement.
questions.expected_answer: Opening carrying value: R1 400 000 less R560 000 is R840 000. Add additions at cost, R400 000. Deduct the disposal at carrying value: R200 000 less R140 000 is R60 000. Deduct depreciation of R230 000. Closing carrying value: 840 000 plus 400 000 less 60 000 less 230 000 — R950 000. Verify by columns: closing cost is 1 400 000 plus 400 000 less 200 000, R1 600 000; closing accumulated depreciation is 560 000 plus 230 000 less 140 000, R650 000; and 1 600 000 less 650 000 confirms R950 000. The income statement separately reports a loss on disposal of R12 000 — proceeds of R48 000 against the carrying value of R60 000. The note records only the carrying value leaving; the selling price never enters the note, and note, bank and income statement must reconcile as a triangle.

questions.question: Equipment cost R900 000, depreciated straight-line at 10 percent per year, with accumulated depreciation of R630 000. Interpret the age and remaining lifespan, make a management recommendation, and explain how comparing additions with depreciation reveals the replacement rate — including the cautions a strong answer states.
questions.expected_answer: The annual charge is 10 percent of R900 000, R90 000, implying a ten-year lifespan. Average age: accumulated depreciation divided by the annual charge — R630 000 over R90 000 — seven years, leaving three years of expected life. Recommendation: plan replacement now — budget, arrange finance and schedule purchases across the remaining three years — rather than meeting the full bill when the equipment dies. Replacement rate: compare additions with depreciation; Bathini added R400 000 against depreciation of R230 000, so capacity is being renewed faster than it is consumed. The reverse pattern sustained over years means the business is eating its capacity while looking profitable, because little is spent — until breakdowns, downtime and safety problems arrive. Cautions: these figures are averages across the class, so one new item can mask several old ones; fully depreciated assets still in use distort the calculation; and the age formula assumes the straight-line charge — under diminishing balance the charge shrinks yearly, so age must be estimated from carrying value against cost instead.

questions.question: Contrast internal and external auditors on appointment, reporting line, timing, scope and purpose; describe the kinds of audit evidence and the three sampling techniques; and explain the structure of an internal audit finding and where accountability for fixing weaknesses lies.
questions.expected_answer: Internal auditor: an employee, appointed by management or the board, reporting to management and the audit committee, working all year, with a broad scope over any control or process, aiming to improve the company's own controls. External auditor: independent and in public practice, appointed by the shareholders at the annual general meeting, reporting to the shareholders, working principally at year-end, with a focused scope — the annual financial statements — and the purpose of giving outsiders a trustworthy opinion on fair presentation. Strong internal work can reduce external testing, but the external auditor never simply adopts internal findings. Evidence, strongest first: physical inspection, documentation, observation of processes, enquiry and confirmation, and recalculation — independent, documented evidence beats verbal assurance. Sampling: random gives every item an equal chance; systematic takes every nth item for coverage; stratified or judgement sampling weights toward high-value and high-risk items, and auditors combine them. A finding states the gap between what should happen and what does, the risk in rands, and the recommendation. Internal audit reports weaknesses; management is accountable for acting — accountable management of resources means management answers for what happens next, with the audit committee and external auditor as backstops.
